channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: open-source paint archive explores reusable biomaterials and earth pigments for fine art
item.description: designboom: “The Experimental Paint Archive by Sophia Collender is a publicly accessible and open source collection of biodegradable, non-toxic, and reusable fine art materials. The history of paint is entwined with a history of material experimentation, and of people who have often taken considerable financial, physical, and environmental risks in order to attain specific visual effects.”

item.title: New database compares rent costs at Maine’s mobile home parks
item.description: News Center Maine: “The Maine Office of Community Affairs has launched a dashboard with data on Maine’s 475 mobile home parks, including how much lot rent is at each of them. It’s a new tool to try to protect mobile home park residents, as more parks are bought by large, out-of-state corporations that often raise rent.”

item.title: PCVR Central Has 898 VR Mods in One Catalog, and It Labels the Rough Ones
item.description: VR.org: “PCVR Central is a catalog. It currently holds 898 VR mods covering 874 of the 1,504 flat PC games it tracks, and its entire pitch is that it tells you which of those mods are actually any good before you spend an evening installing one.”

item.title: Meta rejects claims it sought to hook children to Facebook, Instagram
item.description: Reuters: “Four lead states — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — accused Meta of designing Facebook and Instagram to hook young users, fueling anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misleading consumers about the platforms’ safety. All 29 states accused Meta of violating federal law by improperly collecting and using children’s personal data. Experts have called the trial in the Oakland, California, federal court, which began with opening statements on Tuesday, the biggest legal test yet of social media’s effects on young users.”

item.title: Google Begins Rolling Out The August 2026 Spam Update
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Google has begun rolling out the August 2026 spam update, according to the Search Status Dashboard. The rollout applies globally and to all languages, and Google says it may take a few days to complete…. As of publication, Google hadn’t posted a blog article to go with the dashboard note. Its spam updates page hasn’t changed since December.”

item.title: Google Just Made It Easier for Campaigns to Send You Fund-Raising Emails
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Google quietly rolled out a new program on Monday that will allow candidates, political parties and political action committees to more easily bypass Gmail’s spam filter and send fund-raising appeals to the inboxes of the company’s many millions of email users.”

item.title: Stars and Stripes publisher announces retirement
item.description: Stars and Stripes: “[Max D.] Lederer said he decided to step down because it had become clear that his philosophy of leadership and ‘understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes’ differed in ‘fundamental ways’ from plans the Defense Department has for the organization.”

item.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “[Seth] Rudetsky had stumbled into an increasingly sophisticated scam in which fraudsters impersonate famous podcasters and their representatives, using flattering, highly personalized invitations — most likely composed by AI — to lure prospective guests into handing over money, login credentials or control of social media accounts.”

item.title: Reaching the End of My Selfie a Day for a Year Project
item.description: Faraway, So Close: “As I write this on Monday, August 17th, there’s two more ‘selfie of the day’ posts left for me to do before wrapping up the project. I thought I’d do a bit of a review of my thoughts about this project, as well as write about my plans for what I’m doing for the next daily project when this is over.”

item.title: Collections Highlight: Digitizing the Lautman Collection
item.description: National Building Museum: “In 2007, the National Building Museum received [Robert C.] Lautman’s business archive of architectural photography materials, estimated at over 70,000 objects. Today, Museum staff are working to organize, catalog, rehouse, and digitize the collection to improve public access and ensure its long-term preservation.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Have you been Flocked? This website lets you find out
item.description: Mashable: “A website called Have I Been Flocked? lets you enter your license plate number and check whether it appears in publicly released records of searches conducted through Flock Safety’s system. As of Aug. 17, the website had compiled nearly 242 million searches involving more than 4.6 million plates.”

item.title: About
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: XCancel. From the page: “Using an instance of Nitter (hosted on a VPS for example), you can browse Twitter without JavaScript while retaining your privacy. In addition to respecting your privacy, Nitter is on average around 15 times lighter than Twitter, and in most cases serves pages faster (eg. timelines load 2-4x faster). In the future a simple account system will be added that lets you follow Twitter users, allowing you to have a clean chronological timeline without needing a Twitter account.”

item.title: Raclin Murphy Museum of Art launches a new free Digital Guide to the Museum’s collections
item.description: Raclin Murphy Museum of Art: “The Raclin Murphy Museum of Art is delighted to launch a new digital guide in partnership with Bloomberg Connects, the free arts and culture app…. With origins dating to 1875, the Raclin Murphy Museum of Art (formerly Snite Museum of Art) is one of the oldest and most highly regarded university art museums in America. The renowned permanent collection contains more than 31,000 works representing many cultures and periods of world art history.”

item.title: Governor Katie Hobbs Launches AI Tool to Make Government Work Better for Arizonans
item.description: State of Arizona: “Today Governor Katie Hobbs launched FindServices.az.gov, a centralized, artificial intelligence-powered search tool that simplifies how Arizonans find and learn about government resources. In Arizona, there are over 60 Departments, Agencies, Boards, and Commissions offering more than 300 programs designed to protect consumers’ health, safety, and wellbeing. This website is a one-stop shop for these consumer protection resources and many other state services.”

item.title: Reddit is experimenting with video and audio versions of posts
item.description: Engadget: “Reddit is known for not really changing much about its core features. It even maintains (for now) a 21-year-old version of its site for longtime users who want everything to always look the same. But now the company is testing whether people want to experience posts and comments without having to read walls of text.”

item.title: Discord halts livestreams in Brazil after watchdog cites child safety failures
item.description: Associated Press: “In July, an underage girl in the state of Mato Grosso do Sul was allegedly coerced by other users into committing suicide during a livestream on the platform, putting the company under increased scrutiny. Brazil’s first lady Rosângela Lula da Silva, known as Janja, said on Aug. 6 that the platform should be taken offline, citing the case.”

item.title: Feedly attributes weeklong slowdown to bug, not its AI pivot
item.description: TechCrunch: “Bad news for those who get their updates through RSS feeds: Feedly, the largest stand-alone RSS reader worldwide, has experienced technical issues for over a week, and paying users are upset that the web app has been ‘unusably slow.’ Some users have also reported that the company has ignored their support requests. Uh-oh.”

item.title: Can this treasured S.F. photography institution cheat death again?
item.description: Mission Local: “Hal Fischer says he’s twice rescued SF Camerawork, the nonprofit gallery that has supported the work of experimental photographers for over 50 years, and he’s ready to do it again.”

item.title: ABC Unveils New Twist for Live-Streamed News: Shows That Respond to Viewer Queries, Needs
item.description: Variety: “During a recent live-stream of ‘Searched’, a relatively new entry to the schedule of ABC News Live, Benitez, clad in bright white sneakers and a short sleeve shirt, offered followers different angles on top news stories — the ones they were asking about on their own. ‘Searched’ uses data from web queries to determine what stories viewers are most curious about and what questions they truly want answered.”

item.title: Zelensky signed decree on measures to protect Ukrainian national landmarks
item.description: Ukrinform: “President Volodymyr Zelensky signed a decree on nationwide measures to protect Ukrainian national shrines. According to Ukrinform, he announced this during an event marking the 975th anniversary of the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.”

item.title: Street artist Tom Bob turns the everyday into something extraordinary
item.description: New Bedford Light: “When Tom Bob first got a glimpse at the street artist community, he asked himself, ‘Why not me?’ And he ran with it. Known for his playful style of transforming ordinary objects into whimsical characters, the New Bedford-born and New York-based artist has accumulated a following of over 230,000 Instagram followers. Pipes, vents, parking bumpers, fire hydrants. What most people barely notice walking down sidewalks, Tom Bob sees as an opportunity to tell a story.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Tech Bro Scrapes Anti-AI Photo App Cara, Then Gloats About It
item.description: PetaPixel: “Cara was started by photographer Jingna Zhang in 2023 as a direct result of big tech firms not taking action against AI bots scraping content from websites. In some cases, the platforms are scraping their users’ data for their own benefit, including Meta platforms. Zhang took to Instagram this morning to share news of the scrape, which was done by a Reddit user who posted about his exploits to a subreddit called r/DefendingAIArt.”

item.title: When data centers come knocking, counties should have a ‘wish list,’ officials say
item.description: Southern Maryland Chronicle: “If one thing was clear after the second major panel focused on the issue at the Maryland Association of Counties summer conference, it was that data centers are not going anywhere — at least not any time soon. So counties should start preparing.”

item.title: Kentucky counties struggle with how to regulate data centers
item.description: Forward Kentucky: “In rural Bell County, Kentucky, residents’ activism led to a two-year moratorium on data center construction, while other counties continue to grapple with how to zone and regulate the massive, energy-intensive facilities.”

item.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens, promising a more age-appropriate chatbot
item.description: Associated Press: “The San Francisco-based company says ChatGPT for Teens, which launches Tuesday, is tailored for kids aged 13 to 17 with stronger protections including content restrictions around things like suicide, self-harm and romantic or sexual chats. It also provides homework and study support designed to help students learn rather than spit out answers and school essays.”

item.title: Google Turns On Gemini A.I. for Students Using Its Classroom App
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Google enabled A.I. features for K-12 schools that have allowed student access to Gemini. Until this week, Google automatically enabled Gemini in Classroom only for students 18 or older.”

item.title: Yale School of Medicine Launches New Online Master of Health Science in Medical AI
item.description: Yale School of Medicine: “Yale School of Medicine is launching a new Master of Health Science in Medical Artificial Intelligence, a graduate degree combining flexible online learning with in-person sessions at Yale, designed to train professionals to develop and implement AI tools across clinical and healthcare settings.”

item.title: AI slop is swamping a House office that drafts US laws
item.description: Politico: “Congressional lawyers are struggling to manage a flood of legislative proposals generated using artificial intelligence tools, many of them riddled with errors and shoddy language. The strain on the House Office of Legislative Counsel is increasing as more congressional offices and outside groups rely on generative AI to draft legislation, according to interviews with eight current and former officials who work or have worked with the office.”

item.title: This BlackRock analyst wants to fix journalism. Step one? Skip the journalists
item.description: San Francisco Standard: “In one example of The Dissent’s parasitic approach, [Dakota] Carrasco’s site regurgitated and reduced a 7,000-word investigation of a complex real-estate battle by The Standard’s Sam Mondros into a 400-word summary(opens in new tab) without mentioning the original work at all.”

item.title: ‘I see the incredible promise’: on set of an AI film shoot as new studios embrace controversial tech
item.description: The Guardian: “Near the collonaded entrance to Sony Pictures’ historic Culver City film studio, a tech-powered rival has sprung up this summer. The artists at Promise, a new studio feeding off the potential of AI, can glimpse the lots where Singin’ in the Rain and Men in Black were shot, but no longer do they need to get beyond the studio’s high walls to make their visions come true.”

item.title: I automated my research workflow with open-source AI, and I finally own my data
item.description: How-To Geek: “Online AI services are a great way to search through and parse long documents, but they come with some drawbacks. Your data is held by someone else, you use up tokens or require a subscription to get access, and you need internet access for it to work. By switching to a local-only approach, I can ensure that no sensitive documents can be leaked accidentally, and I don’t have to worry about whether my private data is being used to train cloud models.”

item.title: Her childhood photo. Thousands of explicit images. One woman’s nightmare.
item.description: Washington Post: This link goes to an MSN-syndicated, non-paywalled version of the article. “Jane later learned that her stepfather had created thousands of sexually explicit images of her as a child and traded them online, she said. He manipulated a photo taken when she was about 11, showing her lying on a couch in an oversize T-shirt, the filings claim, transforming it into graphic fake images….Jane’s stepfather made the more than 7,000 fake explicit images of her using the AI chatbot Grok, released by Elon Musk’s company xAI, according to the documents she filed last month in a federal lawsuit against the company.”

item.title: The Tate Brothers’ Lawyer Is on an Aggressive, AI-Riddled Quest to Win Their Release
item.description: Mother Jones: “[Joseph] McBride, a New York attorney representing both brothers, has launched an aggressive, quixotic, and highly public quest to free the Tates and promote a positive image of the two men. He’s using several tools to do so, including podcasting (both on his own, entitled Judgment Day, and through appearances on others’ shows), intense media engagement, a rally outside the jail, verbose tweeting, and, most unusually of all, a flood of AI-generated images released on X and Instagram.”

item.title: What sort of maths are LLMs good at?
item.description: Gowers’s Weblog: “A first remark here is that LLMs are not just good at finding counterexamples: they can find proofs of difficult statements as well. However, it is notable that the most famous problems they have solved have almost all been with counterexamples rather than proofs. That is true of the two problems mentioned above, and also of the Jacobian conjecture and the unit distance conjecture.”

item.title: NASA’s COFFIES Uses AI to Predict Storm-Causing Active Regions on Sun
item.description: NASA: “As humanity looks to the Moon and stars for future exploration, predicting space weather — conditions in space primarily driven by the Sun — is more important than ever. Now, a team of astrophysicists and data scientists with NASA’s COFFIES (Consequence Of Fields and Flows in the Interior and Exterior of the Sun) has developed a novel machine-learning model capable of predicting the emergence of active regions on the Sun up to 12 hours before they appear.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Explore the Newly Digitized Eric E. Sterling Collection
item.description: American Institute of the History of Pharmacy: “The Eric E. Sterling Collection contains documents, publications, speeches, and correspondence from a variety of organizations involved in drug policy discussions and reform efforts. Much of the material was gathered by Eric Sterling during his tenure as Executive Director of the Criminal Justice Policy Foundation, providing insight into the organizations, individuals, and debates that shaped drug policy in the United States.”

item.title: Online database of Riverfront Times articles gets more stories and redesign
item.description: St. Louis Public Radio: “Hundreds of Riverfront Times articles that had disappeared after the alternatively weekly newspaper shut down are being added to a database started by St. Louis archivists. Riverfront Times Database includes articles from 2014 to 2024. The database now includes cover stories, cover galleries and other stories published within that decade.”

item.title: Judge clears Nine PBS to retrieve 70 years of archival TV data — court rules station owns 50TB of data in Iron Mountain servers after host went under
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “There’s light at the end of the tunnel for Nine PBS. We reported last week that the station lost access to 50TB of data representing 70 years of TV history. The issue was that its cloud storage provider went out of business and access to this important set of backups was abruptly cut off. In the meantime, a judge has cleared the way for Nine PBS to retrieve its archival data and programming from Iron Mountain Data Centers.”

item.title: Art Digitization Project Sends Students on an Exploration of the Erie Art Museum’s History
item.description: Allegheny College: “Two Allegheny College students spent the summer in Erie, but forwent Presque Isle views for a dive into an art collection over 8,000 works deep. Through June and July, Angelee Bawek ’27 and Owen Ranus ’27 conducted a community-based research project digitizing works at the Erie Art Museum.”

item.title: Yandex uses fake forest to hide Russian missile battery
item.description: New Voice of Ukraine: “Yandex, a mapping service popular in Russia, has found a new way to conceal military sites. In particular, fragments of forest appeared on a satellite image of an area near the port of Kronstadt, close to St. Petersburg, where a missile battery is located, the Finnish outlet Yle reported on Aug. 17.”

item.title: Maryland tax court voids digital ad tax, orders refunds to Apple, Google and Peacock TV
item.description: Associated Press: “A Maryland state tax court has struck down the state’s first-in-the-nation tax on digital advertising and ordered state officials to repay the tax money already collected from big tech firms.”

item.title: Natural History Museum’s ‘living laboratory’ logs 11 million environmental records in first year
item.description: Computer Weekly: “The Natural History Museum’s (NHM’s) ‘living laboratory’ garden has collected more than 11 million environmental data records in its first year, feeding readings from more than 50 sensors into the Museum’s Amazon Web Services (AWS)-powered Data Ecosystem.”

item.title: National Library of Wales launches Culture and Climate Cymru resource
item.description: Museums Association: “The National Library of Wales has launched Culture and Climate Cymru, a new website and networking platform to help Wales’s culture and heritage sector respond to the climate crisis.”

item.title: Lawrence High student builds prototype to monitor river conditions in real time
item.description: Lawrence Times: “In May, Liam Sturm had an idea, a box of electronics, and a plan to create a network of low-cost water monitors for Lawrence rivers. By late July, the Lawrence High School senior had a working prototype that could measure water temperature, acidity (pH), water clarity (turbidity) and dissolved materials.”

item.title: Nevada’s only Native high school sees a 50 percent hike in graduation rates
item.description: Nevada Independent: “In 2025, the federal Bureau of Indian Education (BIE) saw a record high 79 percent of seniors graduate at schools it runs. Over 50 percent more than 10 years earlier, according to a recent report. Pyramid Lake High School experienced a 50 percent increase in graduation rates between 2019 and 2025. With a population of 305, Nixon is located in Washoe County and is the seat of tribal government of the Paiute Pyramid Lake Indian Reservation.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Archive of Archives
item.description: Glenn M. brought to my attention. (Thank you sir! Good to hear from you.) Based on the GitHub I would guess it launched around March. From the home page: “Archive of Archives is a curated collection of digital archives developed by SHAPE. All are welcome to contribute to the project. Archive submission guidelines can be found on GitHub.”

item.title: Digital Escape Tools
item.description: Found in my Calishat Snaps: From the About Page: “Digital Escape Tools exists to make strong privacy and security choices easier to discover. The web is crowded with pay-to-play lists, opaque rankings, and products that treat users as inventory. This platform takes a different stance: clear categories, editorial context, and a bias toward open source, self-hosting, and tools that publish security practices.”

item.title: Who Is Using AI?
item.description: Another one from the Snaps: From the About page: “Who is using AI? is a free, live world map of where AI coding tools are being adopted — a ‘Global AI Adoption Index’ that lets anyone search their city and see how it stacks up against the rest of the planet.”

item.title: YouTube will now count a view as soon as a video starts playing
item.description: TechCrunch: “YouTube announced on Monday that it’s changing how views are counted on its platform, with a view now counting as soon as a video starts playing or someone enters a live broadcast. Although the Google-owned platform never disclosed how it previously counted views, it was generally understood that a view was counted after a user watched at least 30 seconds of a video.”

item.title: YouTube’s cultural footprint recognised as creators enter archive collection
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “For the first time, 10 content creators have been inducted into the National Film and Sound Archive of Australia (NFSA) in a partnership with YouTube. Among the inductees to be recognised at a Parliament House event today are mathematician Eddie Woo, musician Tash Sultana and independent animation studio GLITCH.”

item.title: Vancouver company rescues archive of Canadian animator who worked on The Beatles’ Yellow Submarine, The Care Bears
item.description: Vancouver Sun: “Animator Norm Drew and Norm Drew Productions may not be household names these days. But in 1986, the Kenora, Ontario-born and raised and Vancouver-based Drew’s archive was acquired by Gordon Stanfield Animation Ltd., recently via a sale at Langley-based Able Auctions.”

item.title: The Iranian YouTube Show Posing Questions Few Dare Ask
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “When the conservative American commentator Tucker Carlson sat down last year for a buzzy interview with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, the unlikely encounter would most likely never have happened without the involvement of a tiny, independent Iranian outlet. Mahdi Ahmadi, the founder of Azad, a six-person team that hosts debates in Tehran and publishes them on YouTube, pitched Mr. Carlson on the idea, he said, and then connected him with the president’s team.”

item.title: The Ukrainian social media channels tracking Russian missiles
item.description: AFP: “The chances of a missile attack on Kyiv that night were around 50%, according to the administrator of a social media channel monitoring Russian air raids. His channel, Aeris Rimor — roughly derived from the Latin for Searcher of the Skies — is one of dozens sending real-time messages about incoming drones and missiles.”

item.title: Google must make it easier to install alternative app stores, judge orders
item.description: Engadget: “Google began distributing third-party app stores through its Play Store earlier this week, but not everyone is happy with the company’s approach. The Verge reports that Judge James Donato, the US District Court judge who oversaw the company’s antitrust case with Epic, believes Google has introduced unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” to the download process and has given the company a week to make changes.”

item.title: Researchers publish tool to rate disinformation defense
item.description: Defence Blog: “Researchers at Monash University have published a capacity maturity model for assessing how prepared a country is to defend itself against disinformation campaigns, backed by a 103-page white paper that lays out the reasoning behind it in far more depth than the university’s public summary of the project disclosed.”

item.title: Turkic states to create unified digital database of archaeological heritage
item.description: Report AZ: “Participants agreed to establish a unified digital database of archaeological heritage. The new program will include joint expeditions and excavations, including at sites along the Great Silk Road and early Turkic monuments. An Electronic Atlas of Archaeological Sites of the Turkic States will also be created, containing information on their locations, history, research findings and academic publications.”

item.title: It Is Past Time for You to Quit Elon Musk’s X
item.description: Public Comment: “That does not mean that everyone who uses X is going to get brainwashed into becoming a Nazi. But propaganda can work on you in subtler ways as well. It can insinuate extreme ideas into the texture of your everyday life. It can create a whole dreamscape for you to sleepwalk through. And the more time you spend in that dreamscape, the greater the odds that it will influence your real-world thinking and decision-making in ways that you will come to regret later.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Who’s Tracking You? Use This New Service to Find Out
item.description: Krebs on Security: “It can be daunting to determine who’s responsible for showing ads on the websites we visit, or who’s harvesting data from the mobile apps we use every day. That information is already semi-public, but it is not easily parsed and traditionally much of it has remained walled away in the hands of large advertising platforms. Not anymore: A powerful and free new service called DecryptAds scrapes and correlates this adtech data and makes it simple to quickly learn a great deal about the entities that are tracking you.”

item.title: Tunney Song Tradition Trust launch unique song collection
item.description: Donegal News: “THE Tunney family, from Letterkenny, in association with Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, launched ‘Where the Linnets Sings 2026’ at Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann in Belfast. It is a unique digital collection of 19 singers spanning five generations and featuring 42 songs made over a 74-year period. Some of the songs have been sung within the family since before the Famine.”

item.title: Over 200 works by Frederic Church digitized for public access in new online portal
item.description: ArtDaily: “The Olana Partnership and the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation (OPRHP) announce the largest launch to date of public online collections for Olana State Historic Site on August 17, 2026. Upon its launch, this resource will feature over 200 records of artwork by the artist Frederic Church, Olana’s creator, and is an important part of the year-long Frederic Church 200 initiative led by The Olana Partnership to mark the 200th anniversary of Church’s birth.”

item.title: FontBase launches Fontalog — the biggest font database in the world with over 3.5 million fonts
item.description: EINPresswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “Fontalog is a searchable, super-fast, free database of fonts, created by FontBase. You can search fonts by visual characteristics, the same way you can do in our SuperSearch: proportion, contrast, weight and xHeight. On every font page there are multiple similar fonts displayed along with foundry info and exact parameter numbers, which you can use to search even more fonts. How did we do this? No AI was used to create this.”

item.title: Castro bars dropped face scanners. The bigger fight isn’t over
item.description: SF Standard: “A months-long fight over an ID-scanning system that photographs arriving patrons at Castro gay bars has come to a head, with all three venues known to use it — Badlands, Toad Hall, and The Mix — halting the practice under pressure from privacy advocates. But the retreat from the tool, PatronScan, hasn’t settled the question at the heart of the fight: whether the added security is worth the privacy trade-off.”

item.title: A smart feeder outage left some cats and dogs without scheduled meals
item.description: TechSpot: “Petlibro users reported that pet feeders, fountains, and litter boxes stopped working properly during a service outage that began on Tuesday. For some owners, the problem went beyond losing app access: they said scheduled feedings did not happen.”

item.title: Carly Simon to open her archives to the public this fall
item.description: Arch Music News: “The Rock & Roll Hall of Famer, whose new album Comes in Waves is out now, is getting ready to open her archives to the public. Simon and her team have been working on her archives for the past nine years. It will give fans insight into her life’s work, and will feature previously unseen photographs and films, as well as unreleased recordings, unfinished songs, lyric sheets, artwork and more.”

item.title: The Government is Monitoring Anti-Flock TikTok and Instagram Accounts
item.description: 404 Media: “Government surveillance centers are monitoring viral anti-Flock Instagram posts, warning local police about upcoming DeFlock events including one scheduled to start next week, and have told cops to ‘increase patrols around ALPR [automatic license plate readers]’ as backlash to Flock grows, according to government intelligence bulletins obtained using public records requests.”

item.title: U.S. Imposes New Import Restrictions on Nepal’s Archaeological and Religious Artifacts
item.description: NepYork: “The United States has imposed new import restrictions on a broad range of archaeological and ethnological materials from Nepal, a move intended to curb trafficking and pillaging of the country’s cultural heritage, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) announced in a final rule published Wednesday.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Archiving Appalachia: One Chattanoogan’s mission to save the musical tapestry of the American South
item.description: Chattanooga Times Free Press: “Chattanooga Folk, a music archival website and repository, has digitized over 2,100 songs thus far in its online catalog, creating new access to music that had exclusively existed in physical form before the project.”

item.title: A new tropical architecture archive traces a unique, global journey across the 20th century
item.description: Wallpaper: “The Architecture Association (AA) has unveiled to the public its Department of Tropical Architecture Archive – an extensive, fascinating and important digital platform documenting projects, pedagogies and legacies springing from its historical namesake academic division, which showcases the powerful impact the department’s graduates had in shaping global architecture.”

item.title: 132 Blaugust posts
item.description: What the Fran: “I visited the Blaugust participants and these are my favourite blog posts from each so far. They’re listed in alphabetical order by blog name. Sadly I only read English so for the blogs in other languages I’ve tried to link something cool. Otherwise they, and other blogs that 404ed or didn’t have any August posts yet, are at the end of the post.”

item.title: These 4 open-source apps solved problems I didn’t think software could fix
item.description: How-To Geek: “Open-source software usually gets recognized for the big, obvious wins, like replacing a cloud storage subscription or a password manager. What gets less attention are the smaller, oddly specific problems that software can fix just as well. Mostly because it doesn’t occur to us that an app exists for it. The picks below fill exactly that kind of gap. Each one is free and open-source, with most being self-hostable.” I’m actually a little annoyed because this article is far better than that mid headline would indicate. I want to try all four of these picks.

item.title: A Google insider spills the tea on how the company forsook its founding ideals
item.description: Ars Technica: “The story of how [Claire Stapleton] went from enthusiastic cheerleader to proactive dissident, and the many lessons she learned along the way, are featured in her new book, Don’t Be Evil: Bad Bosses, Fake Promises, and My Escape from Big Tech—A Biting Memoir of Twelve Years Inside Google.”

item.title: Give Google the boot by building your own search engine
item.description: The Register: “If you’re fed up with search results drowning out the bits of the web you actually care about, you could always build your own search index, as one developer did. Nottingham, UK-based software dev Alex Morley-Finch built the open-source project dubbed Marlin for himself, cataloging around 560,000 homepages for roughly $10 in rented cloud GPU time and using less than a gigabyte of disk storage.”

item.title: After 31 Years, a Quirky Gay Gossip Website Shuts Down
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “At around 5 p.m. on July 30, one day ahead of schedule, the DataLounge, a long-running online forum that became a gathering spot for (mostly) gay men, went dark. Just like that, tens of millions of posts spanning more than three decades simply disappeared.”

item.title: CFPB Pulls Consumer Complaint Narratives From Public Database
item.description: CU Today: “The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Friday said it will stop publishing consumers’ written complaint narratives and related visualizations in its public Consumer Complaint Database, saying the unverified accounts can present a one-sided picture of financial companies and may not involve violations of law.”

item.title: Is There Anyone Who Can Respond to My FOIA Requests? Anyone?
item.description: ProPublica: “According to OPM data, more than 600 government information specialists (staffers who administer FOIA and the Privacy Act) have resigned or been fired since the start of the second Trump administration. Within OPM itself, 12 information specialists left, seven of whom were laid off. (There was one new hire in that time period.) Reached by phone, the former FOIA specialist told me the cuts made the office less efficient, less able to perform its function and threatened the statutory laws they are required to fulfill.”

item.title: States take Meta to trial in California in the biggest fight yet over social media harms to children
item.description: Associated Press: “Of the thousands of lawsuits Meta faces over child safety on its platforms, none may be more consequential than one going to trial this week in California. States are seeking extensive financial damages that could, in theory, total as much as $1.4 trillion, plus changes to how the company operates Facebook and Instagram.”

item.title: Meet the people keeping dialects and heritage languages alive in Singapore
item.description: Channel News Asia: “Beyond the buzz over Teochew box-office hit Dear You, some Singaporeans are determined not to let dialects and heritage languages fall out of use – by teaching, documenting and speaking them.”

item.title: Someone Crammed a Working Windows XP PC Inside a Walnut
item.description: Geeks Are Sexy: “Forget Raspberry Pis, mini PCs, and laptops. Someone looked at a walnut and thought, ‘You know what this needs? Windows XP.’ And instead of immediately questioning that decision, Dr. Kun Dániel spent hundreds of hours turning the walnut into a fully functional computer with a tiny screen, five-button keyboard, USB-C port, and an actual operating system.” Good morning, Internet….

item.title: National Library launches e-database in honor of Khagani Shirvani
item.description: Azernews: “An electronic information database dedicated to prominent Azerbaijani poet Afzaladdin Khagani Shirvani has been presented to users at the Azerbaijan National Library, AzerNEWS reports.”

item.title: Wayne James’ ‘Gift to the People of Cuba’ Preserves a Century of History
item.description: St. Thomas Source: “‘A gift to the people of Cuba’ is how Crucian-born historian, fashion designer and former Sen. Wayne James described his collection of rare photographs donated to the Miami-Dade Public Library System last year. Now, the 1,670-image collection has been fully archived, captioned and digitized, giving the public a glimpse of Cuba as it appeared a century ago.”

item.title: Led by U.S. sales, TikTok Shop is on track to hit $100 billion of gross merchandise value in 2026
item.description: Tubefilter: “Five years ago, TikTok Shop‘s annual gross merchandise value (GMV) totaled less than $1 billion. In 2026, the ecommerce hub is on pace to increase that number a hundredfold. According to data from Momentum Works and Tabcut, TikTok Shop’s 2026 GMV has already surpassed $50 billion, with U.S. sales leading the way.”

item.title: How I turned my Linux desktop setup into a portable package I can run on any machine
item.description: How-To Geek: “I had spent months refining my Linux desktop environment. Every config file had a place, my command line tools were selected for the way I worked, and my desktop shortcuts, panel layout, themes, and custom scripts were configured exactly the way I wanted. I had already automated much of the process. I could clone my repositories, install packages, restore configuration files, and run setup scripts. Even then, rebuilding a Linux desktop from scratch remained a time-consuming process. Instead of rebuilding the system after installing Linux, I wanted to take the system I was already using, turn it into an ISO, and install that environment on another machine. That led me to Penguin’s Eggs.”

item.title: Your McDonald’s File is Probably Bigger Than Your FBI File
item.description: Gizmodo: “Wired reporter Reece Rogers requested the information that the fast food giant had stashed on him, and received a 515-page report that included predictions on how often he’d frequent the restaurant, when and where he was most likely to visit, and what he was most likely to order.”

item.title: That Chrome Update Pop-Up May Actually Be Malware
item.description: Lifehacker: “If you’re seeing pop-ups in Chrome pushing you to download an update in order to continue browsing or avoid losing access to your data, you may be a target for malware. As Android Authority reports, compromised browser extensions appear to be distributing malicious scripts disguised as ‘critical’ security updates.”

item.title: UK study explores virtual reality as a tool for memory recovery
item.description: Spectrum News: “It may not be snowing outside, but inside a virtual reality headset, it is already a winter wonderland. That change of scenery is more than just an escape. University of Kentucky researchers are studying whether virtual reality, gaming and music can help people with cognitive dysfunction.”

item.title: Who are the biggest social media stars in Congress?
item.description: Politico: “POLITICO analyzed social media followings on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook for all sitting members of Congress to see whose hard work to win reach and influence has paid off. For lawmakers who regularly use both an official and personal account, POLITICO deferred to the account with the highest following.”

item.title: Athens is cleaning its all-marble Olympic stadium for the first time in more than a century
item.description: Associated Press: “Athens’ U-shaped Panathenaic Stadium — made entirely of white marble — is getting its first systematic cleaning in more than a century. Rebuilt for the first modern Olympics in 1896, the site is the ceremonial send-off point for the Olympic flame, including for Los Angeles 2028.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Grok Calls for Assassination of Elon Musk, Accusing Him of Pedophilia
item.description: Futurism: “Elon Musk’s “maximum truth-seeking” AI Grok is dropping some nuclear takes about its creator. ‘ELON MUSK WATCHES CHILD PORN,’ the notoriously foul-mouthed chatbot raged on X this Tuesday. Shortly afterwards, as if hyping up a political campaign, it called for violence: ‘ASSASSINATE ELON MUSK 2026.'”

item.title: OpenAI Says Robots.txt May Not Apply To ChatGPT’s Fetch Bot
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “ChatGPT’s page-fetching bot is disallowed by more sites than any other AI bot of its kind. It also reached disallowed pages on more sites than any other bot. OpenAI says robots.txt rules may not apply to it because a person asked for the page.”

item.title: Is the Maine news on your social media feed AI-generated? How you can tell.
item.description: Sun-Journal: “Paywall-free, editorially derelict and tuned for social media engagement, AI local news is exploding online in Maine in the age of the attention-grabbing algorithm and declining trust in legacy media. While some avid news readers are skeptical of these sites, others engage unknowingly, with the sometimes misleading, often inaccurate content. Experts say AI news is straining an already-fraying information ecosystem across Maine and the U.S.”

item.title: The data center industry’s PR blitz is backfiring
item.description: Alabama Reflector: “The public relations push isn’t working, said Jeremy Solomon, president and founder of Learnewable. His company uses AI to analyze government ordinances, moratoria and public comments about data centers, renewable energy and electric transmission projects in each of the nation’s 3,144 counties. Nationwide, approximately one in seven counties now has some form of restriction, Solomon said, and advertising won’t win the public’s trust.”

item.title: Data centers guzzle Arizona’s water and power. We calculated how much
item.description: Arizona Republic: “The Republic found that data centers already operating in the region have a combined capacity of at least 2.3 gigawatts. That’s enough power to serve a medium-sized city composed of 300,000 to 500,000 homes. Planned data centers could bring at least 8.5 additional gigawatts onto the local grid. That’s roughly equivalent to the amount of power it takes to serve 1.3 million to 1.9 million homes. Phoenix has about 630,000 housing units; the broader metro area has a little over 2 million homes.”

item.title: Meta Louisiana Data Center: What the $50 Billion Hyperion Project Means for Electricity Bills
item.description: Baton Rouge Weekly Press: “Meta’s massive Louisiana data center project is becoming about much more than artificial intelligence, economic development and a $50 billion investment. It is becoming a question for Louisiana electricity customers: Who ultimately carries the financial risk of building the enormous power infrastructure needed for Meta’s Hyperion data center in Richland Parish?”

item.title: Google announces Gemini 3.7 Flash just three weeks after previous release
item.description: Ars Technica: “Gemini 3.7 Flash is now rolling out to replace 3.6 Flash, which itself was released only three weeks ago. This new ‘workhorse’ model is supposedly the product of core optimizations and developer feedback, offering improved coding and agentic performance.”

item.title: Ohio schools now required to enforce an AI policy
item.description: Spectrum News: “The state of Ohio now requires all grades K-12 schools to adopt an AI policy. State officials say it allows schools to integrate the software to help students learn and process new material.”

item.title: Chatbots are doing the work of Congress with little oversight
item.description: Washington Post: “Across the Capitol, lawmakers and staffers are using artificial intelligence to write speeches and news releases, sort constituent mail, prepare questions for congressional hearings and draft amendments. Even as politicians are debating how to govern AI for the rest of America, Congress has already settled how it will use the technology: quickly, broadly and with little oversight.”

item.title: Google Opens the Gates of AI Slop Hell
item.description: Gizmodo: “Google Gemini has a new feature: Letting users generate AI slop without visible watermarks to identify it. The official Twitter account for the LLM announced on Friday (news dump, everyone!) that users will soon gain the ability to ‘decide if your image, video, and music creations made with Gemini will have visible watermarks.’ Now it’s a toggle.”

item.title: Google AI Overviews With AI-Generated Images In The Wild
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “A month ago, we reported that Google said it would be rolling out AI-generated images within AI Overviews in Google Search. Well, it seems Google is starting to roll out those AI-generated images in AI Overviews this week.”

item.title: Russian missile uses Nvidia AI chip to help target Ukraine
item.description: The Register: “The Defense Ministry’s Intelligence Directorate (GUR) reported this week that it spotted an Nvidia Jetson Orin module in the remains of a Russian S-71 Monochrome cruise missile. The S-71M is an air-launched weapon with autonomous capabilities that can reportedly search for and engage targets using optical sensors and onboard computing.”

item.title: Connecticut judge says plaintiff hid messages for AI in court filings
item.description: Reuters: “A state judge in Connecticut said a plaintiff in a case before him included ‘hidden text’ in court filings meant to serve as instructions to any AI system reviewing the documents.”

item.title: Volunteer Develops Machine-Learning Tool to Identify Rare Clouds
item.description: NASA: “Certain kinds of clouds are misbehaving – appearing more often and lower in the sky than they used to. To help identify the factors influencing these changes (e.g. shifts in Earth’s long-term weather patterns), scientists have asked people around the world with cameras to submit fresh images of these clouds as a part of the NASA-supported Space Cloud Watch project. Now, one volunteer has developed a new tool to help other Space Cloud Watch volunteers work more efficiently.”

item.title: Fun with AI
item.description: Junk Charts: “‘Dario’ is represented by Claude, and ‘Altman’ by ChatGPT. I made the two models debate each other on a topic of my choosing. At each round, they have the opportunity to concede.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Documenting the Signs and Sign Painters of Bursa, Turkey
item.description: New-to-me, from Blag: “In last week’s ‘BLAG 09 Digital Companion’ I mentioned that there was more to come from Murat Ertürk and his ongoing work documentating the hand-painted signs and sign painters from Bursa, Northwest Turkey. Here he introduces the digital archive, YazıBursa (The Lettering of Bursa), that he has developed with his brother.”

item.title: New Database Catalogs More Than 1,700 Cape & Islands Nonprofits
item.description: Cape News: “The nonprofit directory is accessible through the CCYP website, which also features a full calendar of networking opportunities and events and job and volunteer boards. The nonprofit directory and civic engagement map itself includes an interactive map of Cape Cod and the Islands, pinpointing each nonprofit organization in the region.”

item.title: Flock announces changes amid backlash over its license plate reader network
item.description: Associated Press: “Flock Safety, the surveillance technology company increasingly under scrutiny from lawmakers from both parties, civil liberties advocates and citizens across the U.S., announced Thursday that it is making changes to its platform intended to quell privacy concerns and address documented abuses of its system by some members of law enforcement.”

item.title: Introducing the WordPress Browser Extension
item.description: WordPress: “This new open source extension lets logged-in site users easily hide the admin bar while keeping its most helpful shortcuts in the browser toolbar, provides quick access to all of your WordPress sites, and adds helpful tools for developers and content creators.”

item.title: Google Can’t Promise You’ll Always Have Access to Your Digital Library, but Can Give You a Small Credit
item.description: Gizmodo: “Having your favorite films and TV shows in your digital library is supposed to mean you can access them anytime, anywhere. It actually means being able to access them as long as your digital overlord allows. Polygon recently highlighted how this problem hits consumers, following a Redditor who fought to regain access to The Lord of the Rings: Extended Edition Trilogy after Google removed it from its catalogue and had to settle for a credit to start the cycle all over again.”

item.title: Japanese publishers are fighting imposter news sites with a cryptographic signature
item.description: NiemanLab: “[Originator Profile] isn’t meant to judge whether all of the content on a website is true. It doesn’t authenticate specific photographs or video clips. Instead, it authenticates the site itself — for example, confirming that a news article is genuinely coming from the news organization it claims to be.”

item.title: A new tool for keeping track of your film shots: Frames
item.description: Down the Road: “I’m trying something new. Every so often a software developer reaches out to tell me about a new app they’ve built for film photographers. They’re invariably a film photographer themselves, and they built an app they wanted for themselves. So far none of these apps have entered my workflows — they’ve been fine apps, just not ones that solve problems I have. But I like the idea of putting good work from our community in front of you, because you might find it valuable.”

item.title: White House signing deals with private hackers to combat cybercrime
item.description: Mashable: “In a first for the United States, the White House is looking to build an army of private hackers to combat cyberattacks. Outlined in a new presidential memoranda issued Aug. 12, the Trump administration will begin contracting out efforts to curb the actions of transnational criminal organizations (or TCOs) to American businesses.”

item.title: England and Wales ban Meta Glasses from courtrooms
item.description: Engadget: “Courts in England and Wales have officially banned Meta glasses, according to a report by The Guardian. Anyone trying to enter court buildings with the glasses will have them confiscated and returned when they leave. His Majesty’s Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS), which is responsible for all criminal, civil and family courts, is behind the decision.”

item.title: Op-Ed: Closure of 2 National Archive offices will hurt families
item.description: AsAmNews: “Were my sister not able to retrieve these records of our father and hold them in her hands our families would not know nor understand the scope of his journey nor the depth of his courage in grasping the American Dream. He achieved much of it. And may we build upon it and upon his shoulders. We can do so by keeping these records here at NARA San Bruno, accessible to members of the public and other heirs of history.”

item.title: Reddit Preserved The Part Of The Internet We Broke
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Faster access to information doesn’t automatically create confidence. The next era of the web can’t only be about giving people answers faster. It has to help them understand why an answer should be trusted and let them see the experience behind it.”

item.title: A family reunion drew 500 people to an Omaha park. It’s been going for over 100 years.
item.description: Flatwater Free Press: “Historical matriarch Emma Early Fisher Bryant convened the inaugural family picnic in 1917 in Mandan Park near the original family home in South Omaha as a send-off for sons going to fight in World War I…. Fast forward to today, the family’s ranks include Ph.D.s, CEOs, entrepreneurs, ministers, authors and at least one celebrity — Gabrielle Union.” Good morning, Internet…
